paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 4.23 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 4 (Part 2)
paragraphs.text: (1) An order to provide security for payment of a costs award must, unless the Court otherwise orders, (a) specify the nature of the security to be provided, which may include payment into Court, (b) require a party to whom the order is directed to provide the security no later than 2 months after the date of the order or any other time specified in the order, (c) stay some or all applications and other proceedings in the action until the security is provided, and (d) state that if the security is not provided in accordance with the order, as the case requires, (i) all or part of an action is dismissed without further order, or (ii) a claim or defence is struck out. (2) If the security is given by bond, the bond must be given to the party requiring security unless the Court otherwise orders. (3) If the security is given by money paid into Court, the money may, by agreement of the parties, be paid out and a bond substituted for it. (4) As circumstances require, the Court may (a) increase or reduce the security required to be provided, and (b) vary the nature of the security to be provided. (5) An order under this rule may amend a complex case litigation plan.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 4.23:1 Rule 4.23 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 4.23. 1. Form of Security The court may accept anything reasonable as security, for the form and amount of security are in the “discretion” of the court: Daniell, vol. 1, p. 71; vol. 2, p. 1621. The security might be a bond or payment into court: id., vol. 2, pp. 1621-23; Chitty's Archbold, vol. 1, p. 402; see (English) Supreme Court Practice, 23/1-3/20 and 23/1-3/21. Alberta R. 597 and Seton, 5th ed. (1891), vol. 1, p. 26, expressly contemplate a bond. A bond was allowed in Booth v. Estabrook Const., supra, pp. 167-68. So suggestions that a non-resident plaintiff must pay cash into court are unfounded. If a plaintiff does not escape security because of poverty, then he can offer some kind of security. He might offer a mortgage on his home or farm in Ontario; if any of his friends or relatives will act as sureties, then he can offer their bond. Singh v. Dura (1988), Crothers v. Simpson Sears Ltd., 59 Alta. L.R. (2d) 1 at 13-14 (C.A.). 2. Extensions of Time The court can later extend time to give security, even reviving a suit dismissed for failure to give security: Murray v. Delta Copper Co., [1923] 2 W.W.R. 275 (Alta. C.A.); Columbia Pictures of Can. Ltd. v Gurevitch, [1935] 2 W.W.R. 581 at 582-83, 585-86 (Sask. C.A.). The reference in R. 596 to “special application” reinforces that: Murray case at pp. 287-88; Columbia case at pp. 582, 585-86. So it is unnecessary to cite more general cases. Singh v. Dura, supra, at 14. 3. Refusing to Order a Stay if Security Not Posted The court may choose not to dismiss or even stay the action if the plaintiff does not provide the security ordered …Singh v. Dura, supra, at 14. Practice Note: Otherwise the order must set forth the matters noted in subrules (a)-(c) inclusive. 4. Application for Increased Security One may apply for an increase in costs already incurred. It was argued that security should not be ordered for past costs, and it was pointed out that the defendant had not moved for the increased security until a large amount of costs had been incurred. King's Bench Rule 677 provides that the security shall be of such amount and be given at such times and in such manner as the Court or Judge may direct. This Rule contemplates the making of more than one order for security, and the making of the order at any time. The practice in England is that the application may be made at any stage of the proceedings; it is also the practice there not to confine security to future costs, but to extend the security to costs already incurred in the suit … The practice established by these authorities has been followed in the Courts of this province …Jorgenson v. Reid, [1932] 3 W.W.R. 250 at 254 (Sask. C.A.). In Condominium Corp. No. 0321365 v. 970365 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 471, 2013 CarswellAlta 1674, 568 A.R. 357, Justice Hall set out the test for variation of a security for costs order. At paragraphs 20–22, his Lordship said: 20 Review of the case law in this area indicates that the test for variation of an order for security for costs under Rule 4.23(4)(a) is: (a) whether the plaintiffs have established a material change in circumstances; and (b) whether such material change in circumstances justifies a variation of the amount of security for costs posted. This requires a 2 step consideration: (i) a review of the factors set out in Rule 4.22(a) to (e); and (ii) whether it is just and reasonable to vary the security for costs, having taken those factors into account. 21 Where the Plaintiff is an individual, impecuniosity can be established upon the evidence of the individual. Where the Plaintiff is a limited liability corporation, even though the corporation may itself be impecunious, the Court looks beyond the corporation itself to its shareholders, to determine whether the shareholders are able to raise necessary funds for the litigation. Those shareholders enjoy limited liability, such that, if the corporation ultimately loses the litigation, the shareholders cannot be pursued by the successful defendants to pay the costs of the action, as their liability is limited to the amount of their investment in the shares of the corporation. 22 A condominium corporation is, however, somewhat different. Each condominium unit holder is jointly liable with the condominium corporation, to the extent of his interest in the condominium property. Therefore the debts of the condominium corporation (including litigation costs) are payable by the unit holders up to the extent of their interests. If costs are awarded against the condominium corporation, those costs can be recovered from the unit holders proportionately to those unit holders' interests. However, if some unit holders are unable to pay their share of costs, their share cannot be recovered from the remaining unit holders. 5. Payment by Instalments In Manson Insulation Products Ltd. v. Crossroads C&I Distributors, 2014 ABQB 634, 2014 CarswellAlta 1892, Justice Poelman said, at para. 28: 28 Directing that security for costs be paid by instalments may be appropriate in some cases. Reasons justifying that approach would include the need to accommodate financial circumstances of the plaintiff and ample time before significant next steps are required. In Trimove Inc. v. Servus Credit Union, 2017 ABQB 50, 2017 CarswellAlta 88, 44 C.B.R. (6th) 5, Justice Nielsen said: 109 There has been a trend in recent cases for the Court to permit payment of security for costs in installments: Chic-Hog-O's Social Roast House Ltd v Virvilis Properties Ltd, 2016 ABQB 37, [2016] A.J. No 42.

paragraphs.text: 4.24. Formal offers to settle
paragraphs.heading: Part 4. Managing Litigation

sentences.text: Formal offers to settle

paragraphs.text: (1) At any time after a statement of claim, a claim under the Family Law Act, an application to vary a custody order under the Extra-provincial Enforcement of Custody Orders Act or an originating application to vary a corollary relief order granted by another court under the Divorce Act (Canada) is filed, but 10 days or more before (a) a streamlined trial is scheduled to be heard, (b) a trial is scheduled to start, or (c) an application is scheduled to be heard or considered, one party may serve on the party to whom the offer is made a formal offer to settle the action or a claim in the action. (2) To be valid a formal offer to settle must be made within the period described in subrule (1), be in Form 22 and include the following information: (a) the name of the party making the offer; (b) the name of the party or parties to whom the offer is made; (c) what the offer is and any conditions attached to it; (d) whether or not the amount of the offer is inclusive of interest and, if not, to what date and at what rate interest is payable under the terms of the offer; (e) whether or not the amount of the offer is inclusive of costs and, if not, the amount or scale of the costs and the date to which they are payable under the terms of the offer; (f) the requirements that must be complied with to accept the offer; (g) a form of acceptance of the offer; (h) notice of the costs consequences specified in rule 4.29. (3) Unless a valid formal offer to settle is withdrawn under subrule (4), the offer remains open for acceptance until (a) the expiry of 2 months after service of the offer or any longer period specified in the offer, or (b) the start of a streamlined trial, the start of a trial or the start of a hearing of an application, as the case may be, whichever occurs first. (4) A valid formal offer to settle may not be withdrawn unless (a) the Court first gives permission for the withdrawal, which may be given only if the Court is satisfied that there are special circumstances that justify withdrawal, and (b) the party who made the offer serves written notice of withdrawal on every party who received the offer. Alta. Reg. 143/2011, s. 8; 126/2023, s. 3

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 4.24:1 Rule 4.24 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 4.24. 1. Offer Must Only Relate to Claims in the Pleadings In Beenham v. Rigel Oil & Gas Ltd. (1998), 240 A.R. 122 (Q.B.), the defendant had filed an “offer to settle” for $50,000, but it covered not only the claims made in the pleadings but also unspecified, potential claims between the parties. The offer was not accepted and the action went to trial in which the court awarded judgment in the amount of $25,000. McMahon J. declined to apply Pt. 12 of the rules because he did not know the value of the potential claims which had been included in the offer. At pp. 123-24, His Lordship said: For a compromise to be effective within the meaning of Part 12 of the Rules of Court it must confine itself to matters raised by the pleadings. If other matters are included, it is not possible for a court to determine whether the judgment has surpassed the offer. Here, other “matters arising from, connected to or related to a series of consulting agreements” have not been pleaded nor quantified. For those matters that were plead, the plaintiffs recovered less than the offer. But, I do not know the value of the other potential claims, if any, which the defendants required to be released for the same sum. Thus, the offer cannot be effective within the terms of the Rules. 2. Application of Rule In Anglin v. Resler, 2022 ABKB 631, 2022 CarswellAlta 2434, Justice Lema considered this issue: whether an interlocutory application, on which costs have already bee determined, counts as a ‘step taken in the action’ under R. 4.29(2), thus qualifying for double-costs treatment under R. 4.29(3), with the defendant having made a formal offer (not accepted) and the action dismissed. Justice Lema concluded: [19] I do not read Rules 4.24(2) and (3) this way i.e. as attaching a secondary, or echo, costs effect i.e. to interlocutory applications where costs have already been addressed, expressly or implicitly. … [29] To the extent R. 4.29(2)'s general reference to “all steps taken in the action in relation to the action” is prima facie seen as embracing interlocutory applications featuring already-determined costs consequences, I see R. 10.29(1)'s more specific reference to the costs of an “application” as prevailing, especially with the latter rule factoring out of the “final determination of the … action.” … [35] All to say: where costs consequences have already attached to a given interlocutory step, such as the applications before Gill J. here, Rules 4.24(2) and (3) do not attach extra consequences. [36] Rule 4.24(2)'s reference to “all steps taken in the action in relation to the action” necessarily means steps for which no costs consequences have already been decided. By extension, with such steps excluded in R. 4.24(2), no doubling under R. 4.24(3) is available, with the latter only reaching steps captured by the former. Alberta (Treasury Branches) v. Floral Holdings Ltd. (1990), 73 Alta. L.R. (2d) 283 (Q.B.), at 285, per Mason J. The rule applies to trials not interlocutory proceedings. I am of the opinion that R. 170 is not applicable to interlocutory proceedings … In my opinion, R. 170 is directed and limited in its scope to costs arising out of actions which involve proceedings for trial. 3. The Rule is Not a Complete Code In McAteer v. Devoncroft Developments Ltd., 2003 ABQB 425, 2003 CarswellAlta 654, 340 A.R. 1, 21 Alta. L.R. (4th) 115, Rooke J. said at p. 132: …[W]hile Rule 170, and related rules, attempt to provide a matrix of options for settlement offers bearing costs consequences, I would not purport to hold that they represent a complete code. Indeed, there may be reasons (such as confidentiality) why a party would not wish to make a formal offer of settlement, even when the offer would otherwise comply with the Rules. …[I]t is my view that the Court should be slow to restrict the ways in which parties may try to settle cases with costs consequences, as those consequences encourage parties to settle litigation where a reasonable offer is made and penalizes others for proceeding with unnecessary trials. 4. Calderbank Offers In McAteer v. Devoncroft Developments Ltd., 2003 ABQB 425, 2003 CarswellAlta 654, 340 A.R. 1, 21 Alta. L.R. (4th) 115, Rooke J. defined a Calderbank Offer at footnote 2 on p 123: Calderbank Offers allow a party to make a settlement offer without prejudice to the issues at trial, while giving the party making the offer the right to refer to it on the issue of costs. The name derives from Calderbank v. Calderbank, [1975] 3 W.L.R. 586, [1975] 3 All E.R. 333 (Eng. C.A.), wherein an offer was made by a wife in a matrimonial cause. The husband declined the offer and persisted in the proceedings. Ultimately, the husband recovered a smaller amount than the offer and the wife was awarded her costs after the date of her offer. Rooke J. stated, at p. 133, that a Calderbank Offer is available in Alberta: Accordingly, I find that a Calderbank offer should remain available to counsel in Alberta as one weapon in the case settlement arsenal. At p. 133, his Lordship specifically agreed with the following comment from Higgs v. Fainstein (1992), 72 B.C.L.R. (2d) 24 (S.C.)[which in turn quotes from Ferris v. Kirstiuk (1989), 39 B.C.L.R. (2d) 268 (Co. Ct.)]: … it was appropriate for the defendants collectively through their common counsel to write the Calderbank letter rather than make separate payments in [formal offers], and appropriate for the letter to be considered now, as stated in Ferris, supra, ‘to have an effect upon the question of costs similar to that of an offer to settle, that is, to allow the court in appropriate cases to punish a party for failing to accept a reasonable offer of settlement, thus forcing an unnecessary trial.’ The Court disagreed that the situations to which a Calderbank Offer could apply should be restricted. Rooke J. said at p. 132 of McAteer: … I am cognizant of Veit J.'s decision in [Inkit Ltd. v. Polar Parkas Ltd., [1995] N.W.T.J. No. 119 (N.W.T.S.C.)], to the effect that a Calderbank letter could be used “where the existing Rules do not deal with a particular situation.” To the extent that decision limits the circumstances wherein a Calderbank offer may be relied upon for the purposes of determining costs, I respectfully disagree. In Johnston v. Day (Litigation guardian of), 2015 ABQB 43, 2015 CarswellAlta 186, (sub nom. Quarin v. Prien, 74 M.V.R. (6th) 23, Chief Justice Wittmann gave this explanation of Calderbank offers (at paragraphs 17–19): 17 There are many authorities referencing Calderbank Offers and their effect on judicial discretion. In Horizon Resource Management Limited v Blaze Energy Ltd., 2013 ABCA 139, the Court of Appeal made it clear that a Calderbank Offer remains available to counsel as an effective settlement incentive in terms of cost consequences: para 93. Further, it is an error on the part of a trial judge to suggest that unless there is a Formal Offer, pursuant to the ARC, a Calderbank Offer which does not conform to the ARC in all respects ought not to be considered in terms of cost consequences: para 94. 18 Many authorities seem not to define exactly what a Calderbank Offer is. In Calderbank v Calderbank[1975] 3 ALL ER 333 (CA), a husband and wife were engaged in divorce proceedings and the husband made an application under the Matrimonial Causes Act, 1973 seeking a financial provision or alternatively, a property adjustment order, in his favour. The trial judge made a lump sum order in favour of the husband in the amount of $: 10,000. The costs issue surrounded the trial judge's order that each party should pay his or her own costs. The wife's solicitors had written to the husband solicitors offering something substantially more than $: 10,000 in a without prejudice letter. The Court held that because the letter was written without prejudice, it could not be considered. The Court did hold that it would be possible to put forward an offer, without prejudice to the issue of damages but reserving the right to refer to it on the issue of costs. However, in Calderbank, the wife swore an affidavit offering a house to the husband, the value of which was $: 12,000. In disposing the issue of costs, Cairns L.J. stated at page 343: I have reached the conclusion that that was an offer of which in the circumstances of this case, the husband ought to have accepted and that as he persisted in these proceedings and recovered a lump sum of a smaller amount than the value of that house, the right order would be that he should have the costs up to 14 days after 14th August and thereafter, the wife should have her costs in the proceedings in the court below. 19 In McAteer v Devoncroft Developments Ltd., 2003 ABQB 425, a Calderbank Offer was held to have the same effect as a Formal Offer in terms of cost consequences: para 55. Although costs are always in the discretion of the Court, that discretion must always be exercised judicially. Guidance to judicial discretion in the case of a Calderbank Offer mandates that a valid Calderbank Offer be considered and analyzed in the same manner and to the same extent as a valid Formal Offer to Settle. The substance of the principle is whether the offering party did better at the trial than the terms of settlement offered. In Yellowbird v. Samson Cree Nation No. 444, 2006 ABQB 913, 2006 CarswellAlta 1728, 406 A.R. 100, 68 Alta. L.R. (4th) 255 (Alta. Q.B.), Slatter J. (as he then was), discussed the effect of placing the words “without prejudice” on a Calderbank letter. At p. 259, his Lordship said: 10 The Defendant also made an offer on May 18, 2006. This offer was contained in a letter marked “without prejudice”, and specifically stated that it was not made with respect to any rule of court. The letter did however say that it would be brought to the attention of the Court when costs were considered. Such a letter is commonly referred to as a Calderbank letter: Calderbank v. Calderbank, [1976] Fam. 93, [1975] 3 W.L.R. 586, [1975] 3 All E.R. 333. Offers in a Calderbank letter can properly be considered by the Court in exercising its discretion over costs: McAteer v. Devoncroft Developments Ltd., 2003 ABQB 425, [2004] 4 W.W.R. 667, 21 Alta. L.R. (4th) 116, 340 A.R. 1 at paras. 31-44; Mosher v. Reimer, [2004] A.J. No. 771, 2004 ABQB 496. 11 Counsel for the Plaintiffs objects to the Defendant referring to the Calderbank letter because it is marked “without prejudice”. Communications sent to promote settlement are privileged, whether they are marked “without prejudice” or not. The privilege however does not apply to certain accepted uses of the communication. One is to prove the contents of an agreement of accord and satisfaction, when the communications result in a binding settlement contract. Another exception is when the communication is used to determine an award of costs, at least when the letter specifically states that it will be used for that purpose: Leonardis v. Leonardis, 2003 ABQB 577, 50 Alta. L.R. (4th) 56, 36 C.P.C. (5th) 82, 43 R.F.L. (5th) 144, at para. 3. In Alberta Permit Pro v. Booth, 2008 ABQB 167, 2008 CarswellAlta 348, 459 A.R. 320, 89 Alta. L.R. (4th) 307, Read, J. discussed Calderback Orders. At pp. 321-322, her Ladyship said: 56 It is trite to observe that privileged communications may not be introduced before a court as evidence except in very limited cases. “Without prejudice” communications genuinely intended to reach or provide overtures for settlement and compromise are generally privileged: Abrams v. Grant (1978), 5 C.P.C. 308 (Ont. H.C.J.), I. Waxman & Sons Ltd. v. Texaco Canada Ltd., [1968] 1 O.R. 642, 67 D.L.R. (2d) 295 (H.C.J.). 57 Privileged communications are one of the hallmarks of the solicitor-client relationship, and an attempt to disclose privileged communications without proper reason is a serious breach of a lawyer's duties and obligations. When a lawyer receives in good faith a “without prejudice” communication from another lawyer, that recipient ought be able to rely on that communication remaining confidential. A clear intention is required to properly waive privilege: Ericsson Inc. v. Novatel Inc., 2001 ABCA 199, 286 A.R. 190, at para. 13. 58 Nothing which is written or said without prejudice should be looked at without the consent of both parties, otherwise the whole object of the limitation would be destroyed. See, for example: British Columbia Children's Hospital v. Air Products Canada Ltd.; British Columbia Children's Hospital v. Liquid Carbonic Inc., 2003 BCCA 177, at para. 16, 224 D.L.R. (4th) 23; appeal discontinued, [2003] S.C.C.A. No. 240. 59 While the Offer was marked “without prejudice”, communications sent to promote settlement are privileged, whether they are so marked or not. 60 Privilege however does not apply to certain accepted uses of the communication. One is to prove the contents of an agreement of accord and satisfaction, when the communications result in a binding settlement contract. Another exception is when the communication is used to determine an award of costs, at least when the letter specifically states that it will be used for that purpose: Leonardis v. Battaglini, 2021 ABQB 89, 2021 CarswellAlta 261, Justice Feth, in the context of a family law file dealing with support obligations, gave this summary of the law governing Calderbank Offers: [71] In summary, a Calderbank offer is relevant to the Court's deliberations about whether and to what extent costs should be awarded against the party who did not accept the offer. Caproco Corrosion Prevention Ltd., supra, at 24. The Court of Appeal has said: There is one basic rationale for formal offers. It is to prevent further litigation when one of the parties before trial is content with an amount no more favourable to him than the amount which is right in law. That is so even if the plaintiff will not accept 5 cents less than the proper amount. As just noted, that is not their only aim. Is it one of their aims? These Rules are intended to produce settlement only in one sense. They merely say that a party bears heavier consequences if it gambles and loses. The objective is less costly and more timely resolution of disputes with a concomitant reduction in pressure on crowded courts. C.A.) at para. 5: The rules in Part 12 of the Rules of Court, which bear the heading Compromise using Court Process, have the object of promoting settlement and preventing needless litigation. Either a plaintiff or a defendant may trigger the rules and thereafter place the opposing party at risk at to costs where a reasonable compromise is rejected. A defendant may pay into court or offer to accept judgment. A plaintiff may serve an offer specifying the terms of a proposed settlement. The unreasonable plaintiff will pay [double] the defendant's costs for all subsequent proceedings; the unreasonable defendant will pay the plaintiff double costs after the offer is rejected. 6. Offer Does Not Have To Be Less than Amount Claimed An offer under the rule which is not less than the full amount claimed is still an offer of settlement. In Jones v. Trans America Life Insurance Co. of Canada (1996), 39 Alta. L.R. (3d) 1 (C.A.), at 3, the court said: There is nothing in the Alberta Rules of Court confining formal offers to concessions or to reductions in claim. sentences.text: Acceptance of formal offer to settle

paragraphs.text: (1) For the purpose of this Division, a formal offer to settle an action or a claim in an action may only be accepted in accordance with this rule. (2) At any time a formal offer to settle remains open for acceptance or before a formal offer to settle is withdrawn, a party to whom the offer has been made may accept the offer by (a) filing the offer and the acceptance of it, and (b) serving on the party who made the offer notice that (i) the offer has been accepted, and (ii) the terms of any judgment or order in the offer have been agreed to. (3) After the filing and service, a party may (a) apply to the Court for judgment or an order in accordance with the terms of the formal offer to settle, (b) continue the action in respect of any matter not covered by the judgment or order, and (c) continue the action against any party who is not a party to the settlement.

Acceptance Must Match Offer Master Funduk has also commented on the need for the acceptance to match the offer. In Little Caesar's Pizza of Alberta Inc. v. Tipaskan Development Inc. (1995), 31 Alta. L.R. (3d) 218 (Master), the learned Master said, at p. 224: Nobody today argues that the Defendant cannot make what offer it wants to make. Nobody today argues that the Defendant cannot make an offer which includes the condition found in its offer… Just like the case at common law, an offeree cannot pick and choose. Rule 169 does not let a plaintiff accept those parts of an offer that he likes and ignore (not accept) those parts that he does not like. That is what the Plaintiff tries to do. In its acceptance of the offer the Plaintiff does not accept that which is offered. It only accepts that part of the offer to its liking. It does not accept the final term of the offer, the condition. One merely has to look at the offer and the acceptance to see that they are not complementary. The Plaintiff wants only the money to it part of the offer. Subrule (2) says that the Plaintiff may apply for judgment “in accordance with the offer”… Very simply, the Plaintiff did not accept what the Defendant offered. 2. Shell Canada Products Ltd., 2001 ABQB 389, 2001 CarswellAlta 595, 290 A.R. 166, on February 16, 2000 Shell served KEM with a Rule 169 offer of judgment. However, this court has inherent jurisdiction to interfere with a negotiated settlement where there has been a material nondisclosure. In this instance, there was a material nondisclosure that was not brought to the attention of the defendants until after the settlement agreement was reached. The information that came to light after the settlement agreement was relevant and significant to resolution of the issues raised in the action. The existence of the information that was not disclosed was clearly within the knowledge of the party seeking to rely upon the settlement agreement. I conclude that the nondisclosure was intentional and was relied upon by the defendant to its detriment. I am satisfied that the defendant would not have made the settlement offer had it been aware of the information that was subsequently brought to its attention. In dismissing the appeal, Russell J.A., speaking for the majority [see: (2003), 330 A.R. 153 (C.A.)], said, at p. 155: Rule 169 is not intended to impose settlements upon unwilling parties. To deny revocation despite material nondisclosure would discourage reasonable offers of settlement and defeat the intent of that rule. 3. Acceptance of Offer The acceptance must match the offer. Rule 170 permits the plaintiff to serve upon the defendant “an offer specifying the terms on which he is willing to settle the claim”. This encompasses both payment of money and a judgment … The plaintiff contends that by using the term “payment” in his offer to settle, the defendant must accept by utilizing R. 170(2)(a) … If the defendant were to have initiated the settlement process, he could have either paid a sum of money into court under R. 166 or offered a judgment under R. 169. The plaintiff having initiated the procedure, the defendant can either pay the sum offered into court under R. 170(2)(a) or make a confession of judgment under R. 170(2)(b). The defendant's choice must surely be responsive to the plaintiff's offer. The plaintiff's use of the word “payment” corresponds with R. 170(2)(a) rather than R. 170(2)(b). Chendria v. Cucheran (1989), 71 Alta. L.R. (2d) 185 (Q.B.), at 189-90, per Murray J. In 421990 Alberta Ltd. v. Royal Trust Corp. of Canada (1995), 30 Alta. L.R. (3d) 404 (Master), Master Quinn considered an application to withdraw an offer to settle made pursuant to R. 170 even though it had purportedly been accepted by the defendant. During the course of the application, the plaintiff submitted that the offer had not been accepted in the manner set out by the offer. One infers from the judgment that the offer contemplated payment to the plaintiff. The defendant purported to accept it by payment into court. At p. 406, the learned Master made the following comments about the extent to which the acceptance must accord with the offer: Counsel for the plaintiff also submits that a defendant purporting to accept a plaintiff's offer of settlement must be responsive to the terms set out in the offer and that by paying the funds into court rather than to the plaintiff, the defendant has not accepted the offer. In my opinion there is no merit in that argument. It is a matter of form not of substance. It is likely the plaintiff would say the defendant was not complying with R. 170 if the defendant had paid the funds directly to the plaintiff. The learned Master then went on to consider the Notice of Acceptance of Offer, and Certificate of Payment into Court utilized by the defendant to accept the R. 170 offer. The Certificate of Payment indicated that the defendant was paying the funds into court “as security, in accordance with Rule 170(2)(a) of the Alberta Rules of Court”. As to whether that was proper acceptance of the offer, Master Quinn said, at pp. 406-407: The notice of acceptance of offer of settlement filed by the defendant's lawyers does not contain the words “as security” but the presence of those words in the certificate of payment into court, in my opinion, creates a serious problem. Here if the plaintiff had been willing to accept the money in court it seems likely it would have had difficulty actually obtaining the money because of confusion arising from the words “as security”. Moreover it seems to me the inclusion of those words signify an attempt by the defendant to qualify in some way its acceptance of the plaintiff's offer. In my opinion, the defendant's notice of offer of settlement is so compromised by the words “as security” in the certificate that the notice itself was not an effective acceptance and that the plaintiff's withdrawal of the offer after the expiration of the mandatory 45-day waiting period would be a valid withdrawal of the offer. 4. Offers on Multi-issued Lawsuits Speaking for myself, if one makes an offer of settlement on a multi-issued lawsuit and intends each paragraph of the offer to be a separate offer that can be accepted while the other terms are all rejected, one should say so right in the offer …Westersund v. Westersund (1993), 157 A.R. 276 C.A., at 278, per Kerans J.A. 5. Unilateral Mistake In 421990 Alberta Ltd. v. Royal Trust Corp. of Canada (1995), 30 Alta. L.R. (3d) 404 (Master), the plaintiff made a R. 170 offer of settlement. In error the offer did not take into account a significant claim for interest. The plaintiff's lawyer told the defendant's lawyer of the error and said that the plaintiff was withdrawing the offer. The 45-day period under R. 170(5) had not yet expired, and the defendant purported to accept the offer. Master Quinn held that no settlement agreement had been reached because the defendant knew that the offer had been made under a unilateral mistake. At pp. 407-408 the learned Master said: Re Lem Estate (1987), 16 C.P.C. (2d) 139 (Ont. Surr. Ct.), is a case in which Haley Surr. Ct. J. held there had been a unilateral mistake and that no agreement of settlement had been reached. He held it was unreasonable for the applicant (the offeree) to “snap up” an offer she knew or ought to have known was made under a mistake. At pp. 144-45 the learned judge said: The law with regard to mistake is not easy. As stated in Cheshire and Fifoot's Law of Contract (10th ed., 1981) at p. 199: The first fact to appreciate in this somewhat elusive branch of the law is that the word “mistake” bears a more restricted meaning in professional than in popular speech. The learned author identified three types of mistake: common, mutual, and unilateral. He defines each and discusses the cases applicable to each. His thesis is that with regard to common mistake an agreement is actually made between the parties which may or may not be enforceable depending on the particular circumstances. With regard to mutual and unilateral mistake however, his position is that no contract has in fact been made because the parties are never ad idem. The author offers examples of mutual and unilateral mistake as follows: In mutual mistake, the parties misunderstand each other and are at cross-purposes. A, for example, intends to offer his Ford Cortina car for sale, but B believes that the offer relates to the Ford Zephyr also owned by A. In unilateral mistake, only one of the parties is mistaken. The other knows, or must be taken to know, of his mistake. Suppose, for instance, that A agrees to buy from B a specific picture which A believes to be a genuine Constable but which in fact is a copy. If B is ignorant of A's erroneous belief, the case is one of mutual mistake, but, if he knows of it, of unilateral mistake. The approach of the court to mutual and unilateral mistake differs. For mutual mistake the court applies what might be called an objective test, i.e., would a reasonable man in the circumstances decide that an agreement had been reached between the parties. In the case of unilateral mistake the party making the mistake is allowed to show that the effect of that mistake on his own mind as opposed to the mind of a reasonable man. In cases of mistake the court is often influenced in its conclusions by whether or not innocent third parties have relief upon the existence of an agreement between the other parties. On the facts before me no third party has changed his position relying on any agreement between these parties. And at pp. 147-48 he said: In cases of unilateral mistake the court will not permit the other party to ‘snap up’ an offer which he knows to have been made under a mistake, see Hartog v. Colin & Shields, [1939] 3 All E.R. 566 and McMaster University v. Wilchar Construction (1971), 3 O.R. 801; affirmed on appeal without written reasons (1973), 12 O.R. (2d) 512n (Ont. C.A.). … In my opinion there was a “snapping up” by the defendant and for the same reasons as stated in Re Lem Estate (supra) I find that no agreement of settlement was ever reached between the parties.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 4.28:1 Rule 4.28 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 4.28. If Court Reserves Judgment At the conclusion of a trial, the court may reserve judgment. How does one deal with the matter of a payment-in as it may relate to costs without offending R. 173? If the judgment result raises the costs question, one answer is to apply by notice of motion after receipt of the judgment and before entry for an amendment of the judgment regarding costs. In Bazley v. Langmann (1969), 67 W.W.R. 337 (B.C. S.C.), the court said at pp. 339-40: How can a defendant comply with [R. 173] and yet leave the door open so that, if judgment is given against him with costs, he can properly draw to the court's attention the fact that a larger sum had been paid in than the plaintiff recovered? … There may be more ways than one in which the problem can be properly and easily overcome, but the simplest I know of was that adopted by counsel for the defendant in Picard v. Wiebe (No. P 916/62, New Westminster registry, unreported). The facts, in so far as they relate to the problem I am discussing, may be stated very simply. On December 24, 1963, Branca, J. (as he then was) handed down written reasons for judgment awarding the plaintiff judgment for $17,630.15 and costs. The defendants had made two payments totalling $20,442.41 into court pursuant to M.R. 264, of which payments Branca, J. was, of course, unaware. Before the formal judgment was entered counsel for the defendants gave quite informal notice of motion by way of praecipe, as follows: “Motion to the Hon. Mr. Justice Branca re costs, a payment having been made into Court in an amount exceeding the Plaintiff's recovery.” On the hearing of the motion on February 5, 1964, the notices of payment into court were brought to the attention of the judge who made the same direction as to costs as was made in Worrall v. Northwestern Mutual Insur. Co. (No. 2) (1963), 44 W.W.R. 540 (B.C.) without giving further reasons in writing. The formal order (in so far as it dealt with costs) is, however, eloquently simple. Par. 2 provided: And On Motion made this day by the Defendant that the said judgment be varied insofar as it dealt with costs, And Upon Reading the Notices of Payment into Court dated and filed the 6th day of May and the 5th day of December, 1963; And Upon Hearing Counsel aforesaid. Picard v. Wiebe may not offer the only way a defendant can comply with the requirements of M.R. 264 and yet obtain the benefit available under the Rule where he has paid more into court than the plaintiff recovers—but it is certainly one way.

paragraphs.text: 4.29. Costs consequences of formal offer to settle
paragraphs.heading: Part 4. Managing Litigation

sentences.text: Costs consequences of formal offer to settle

paragraphs.text: (1) Subject to subrule (4), if a plaintiff makes a formal offer to settle that is not accepted and subsequently obtains a judgment or order in the action that is equal to or more favourable to the plaintiff than the offer, the plaintiff is entitled to double the costs to which the plaintiff would otherwise have been entitled under rule 10.31(1)(a) or 10.32 for all steps taken in relation to the action or claim after service of the offer, excluding disbursements. (2) Subject to subrule (4), if a defendant makes a formal offer to settle that is not accepted and a judgment or order in the action is made that is equal to or more favourable to the defendant than the offer, the defendant is entitled to costs for all steps taken in the action in relation to the action or claim after service of the offer. (3) A defendant is entitled to double the costs provided for in subrule (2), excluding disbursements, if (a) subrule (2) applies, and (b) the action or claim that is the subject of the formal offer to settle is dismissed. (4) This rule does not apply (a) if costs are awarded under rule 10.31(1)(b), (b) in the case of a formal offer to settle made with respect to a streamlined trial, if the offer is made less than 10 days before the date scheduled to hear the streamlined trial, (c) in the case of a formal offer to settle made with respect to any other matter, if the offer is made less than 10 days before the date scheduled for the trial to start, (d) in the case of a formal offer to settle that is withdrawn in accordance with rule 4.24(4), or (e) if in special circumstances the Court orders that this rule is not to apply.
